entities.name: Andrew of Crete
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Andrew of Crete (c. 650 – July 8, 740), initially known as Andrew of Jerusalem, established himself as a pivotal figure in Byzantine hymnography and theological discourse during the tumultuous 8th century. His career spanned significant political and religious shifts, from his early life in Damascus under Umayyad rule to his later episcopal service in Crete within the Byzantine Empire. Venerated as a saint in both the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches, Andrew's enduring legacy rests predominantly on his innovative contributions to the liturgical poetry of the Orthodox tradition, particularly the development of the 'Great Canon'.

Born in Damascus, Andrew entered the Mar Saba monastery near Jerusalem at a young age, where he received a rigorous theological education. He served as a deacon in Constantinople, holding the position of Orphanotrophos, responsible for orphanages and charitable institutions, from approximately 685 to 692. Andrew participated as a delegate to the Quinisext Council (Council in Trullo) in 692, endorsing its canons, which sought to address disciplinary issues and supplement the Fifth and Sixth Ecumenical Councils. Around 700, he was consecrated Metropolitan of Gortyn and Crete, a role that saw him actively engaged in the ecclesiastical administration and spiritual leadership of the island, then a vital outpost of Byzantine power.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Andrew of Crete fundamentally reshaped Eastern Christian liturgical practice through his pioneering development of the canon, a hymnographic form that replaced earlier traditions and continues to define Lenten worship across Orthodox churches. His 'Great Canon' remains one of the most significant and widely used compositions in Byzantine hymnography.
